source.description: Covariate models for mechanical parts: each part's failure rate is a base rate scaled by factors for the conditions it works in (load, speed, temperature, pressure, contamination, material and more), with the handbook's limits on every input. Seals, springs, solenoids, valves, bearings, gears, actuators, pumps, filters, brakes and clutches, compressors, electric motors, accumulators, fasteners, couplings, slider cranks, sensors, shafts, belt and chain drives, fluid conductors and miscellaneous parts.
caveats: CDNSWC (the Naval Surface Warfare Center, Carderock Division) and the U.S. Navy did not take part in making Reliafy and do not approve it. The handbook is the result of a research programme, not an official DoD document.
A handbook prediction model, not failures counted in service: never mix it with field data.
Each model is only as good as the conditions you give it. Outside the handbook's limits Reliafy refuses or warns, and says which limit and on which page.
The handbook says its equations were validated only in part, with limited funding: use it to compare designs and find the weak parts, not as a measure of how your equipment will fail.
Some rates are per million cycles or operations, not hours: a prediction needs how many there are an hour.

records.notes: Surface finish and hardness change with time in service (p. 3-7): evaluate at several ages for a rate over the product's life. Between Table 3-3's 50 °F steps C_ν is interpolated linearly. The handbook's Table 1-1 example (p. 1-12: seal 1.20, spring 1.04, poppet 0.35 per million hours) uses Chapter 1's physical equations (the leakage form, Eq. 3-5 here, with K1 = 3.27×10⁻⁴); this record uses the chapter's factor model, Eq. 3-7, normalised to field failure data, which isn't algebraically the same: for Table 1-1's seal it gives about 1.5 before C_T and C_N, which Table 1-1 doesn't have. Table 1-1 was also last revised before this chapter (p. vii). The contaminant factor C_N = (C_o/10)³ · FR · N10 (Table 3-4) is usually well below 1 (0.17 for a 10 gpm piston pump and a 10 µm filter, 0.004 for a sliding valve) and is the largest lever in the model; Table 1-1's worked example leaves it out.

Its failure rate is a small base rate plus a rate for each stress (around the wall, along it, and through a thick wall), from how far the mean stress sits below the mean strength given how much each varies, spread over the period you give.

derived.name: eta_l
derived.label: Longitudinal joint efficiency
derived.expr: 1.0 if joint_l == 'none' else (0.55 if joint_l == 'riveted_lap_single' else (0.65 if joint_l == 'riveted_lap_double' else (0.75 if joint_l == 'riveted_lap_triple' else (0.65 if joint_l == 'riveted_butt_single' else (0.75 if joint_l == 'riveted_butt_double' else (0.85 if joint_l == 'riveted_butt_triple' else (0.9 if joint_l == 'riveted_butt_quadruple' else (0.75 if joint_l == 'welded_butt_single' else (0.85 if joint_l == 'welded_butt_double' else (1.0))))))))))
